Castle of Durham, on the 15th of June, 1863, Snt William 
Lawson, Bart., in the chair — it was 

Resolved, That a Third Volume of the Testamenta 
Eboracen8IA should be prepared by the Secretary, as one of the 
Publications of the Society for 1864.

THE PREFACE 



A third volume of Wills from the Registry at 
York is submitted to the members of the Surtees 
Society. The period of time that it covers, counting 
from the date at which its predecessor ends, is only 
eighteen years. The number and value of the docu- 
ments preserved at York make a slow progress neces- 
sary. A large space, also, has been devoted to several 
Inventories of a very earlv date which have been 
recently discovered. The rarity of these lists is only 
equalled by their value. Several will appear in a 
fourth volume, including a magnificent one of Arch- 
bishop Savage. 

It is unnecessary, perhaps, to speak of the value 
and the use of testamentary documents. The light 
which they throw upon language, religious customs 
and observances, and the manners and life of our 
forefathers, is very great indeed. With regard to 
genealogy, it is not too much to say that the three 
volumes of Yorkshire Wills that are already pub- 
lished, build up or reconstruct the pedigrees of the 
gentry of that great county. The Editor has ap- 
pended to the present volume a list of the Marriage 
Licences, &c, recorded in the Northern Registers. 
He hopes to be able to publish from the same 
sources, on some future occasion, a full catalogue 
of the Indulgences and Licences for Oratories which 
were granted in the North of England. 



Digitized by Google 



vi 



It is the chief object of the Surtees Society, not to 
write history, but to supply the materials out of which 
it can be constructed. The members, however, at all 
times take a great interest in the use, which is being 
constantly made, of the publications of the Society. 
They will be much gratified to hear that considerable 
additions are to be made to the printed works on the 
topography of Yorkshire. The counties of Durham and 
Northumberland have found many chroniclers, but the 
vastness of Yorkshire has deterred almost every one 
from attempting to elucidate its annals in a similar 
manner. The author of the History of South York- 
shire is an illustrious exception ; but his is the only 
work that can be spoken of with any respect, as far 
as accuracy and research are concerned. The Editor 
is most happy to announce that there will soon be 
a continuation of the works on Yorkshire topography 
which, in size at least, will range with Mr. Hunter's 
invaluable volumes. The Editor believes, that, if pro- 
perly qualified writers could be found, there would 
be no lack of funds to complete on one plan and in 
one form the history of the whole of Yorkshire, so 
great is the spirit of the gentlemen of that noble 
county. These results are partly owing to the pub- 
lications of the Surtees Society, and the members may 
well be proud of them. The Editor begs them, in the 
name of the Society to which they belong, to assist 
and help on the great work that is in progress. 

J. R. 

York, June 18C5.

On the 5th of November, 1362, be was collated to the vicarage of Mattersey. (Reg.

* A great and wealthy ecclesiastic. 

On the 14th of March, 1379, Mr. Thomas de Dalby, rector of Barking, exchanged 
his living with Laurence de Nayrer for the rectory of Alderton, in the diocese of Nor- 
wich, and the prebend of Welton Beckhall, at Lincoln. (MSS. Had. 6952, 146.) On 
the 5th of October, 1383, he was presented by John lord Love! to the rectory of 
Weatley, co. Stafford. (F.R.R.) This he exchanged in 13S6 for the living of Cot 
ten ham, co. Cambridge, which he exchanged again with Thomas de l'attesle for the 
archdeaconry of Ely, to which bo was collated May 28th, 1387. He was also rector 
of Stretham, near Ely, and prebendary of Salisbury. (Bcntham's Ely, 275.) In Sept. 
1388, the king appointed him to the archdeaconry of Richmond, at York, and he gave 
op that of Ely. (Le Neve, iii. 139.) He was again admitted to Richmond by the 
chapter, during the vacancy of the see, on the 5th of March, 1396-7. (Reg. Dec. et 
Cap. ude uunnte, 2076.) On the 18th of February, 1389, he exchanged his stall 
of Welton at Lincoln with Robert de Dalton for the prebend of Tockerington at 
York. (MSS. Harl. 6952, 256.) Dalby was a canon residentiary at York. 

Dalby made his will on the 16th of May, 1400, and it is printed in the l ent. Ebor., 
i. 261 — 4. It was also registered at Canterbury. In the nave of York Minster was " a 
blue marble, about three yards long, escocheoned at corners, with a coat of arms, a 
chevron between three buckles, and at the head a square plate, with the inscription." 
(MS. Torre on York Minster, 153.) Dalby died on the 19th of May, 1400. (Le Neve, 
iii. 139.) In accordance with his last will, a chantry was founded at the altar of 
8S. Agatha, Lucy, and Scholastica, in York Minster, on Jan. 20th, 1409-10, for 
the souls of archdeacon Dalby, archbishop Arundel, Richard Asty, and Isabel his 
wife, and Sir Philip de Beauchamp. It was worth twelve marks per annum. (York 
Fabric Rolls, 276.)

III. THE WILL AND INVENTORY OF JOIIN DE SCARLE, SOME- 
TIME LORD CHANCELLOR OF ENGLAND. 

[Reg. Test. Dec. et Caph, Ebor., i. 1336, and Orig. Inv.] 

April 22, 1403. Johannes de Scarle^ clericus — sep. in cccl. 
mea S. Briffidae London, si hac vice obire me contigerit. Fa- 
bricae eccl. de Holme-juxta-mare, Norwycensis dioccsios, sive 
emendationi librorum et ornamentorum ejusdcm ccclesiaj, v mar- 
cas; ct emendationi cancclli cjusdem eccl. ij marcas. Fabricae 
ccclesise B. M. de South-Kelsey, sive emendationi librorum et 

* Dilapidations claimed by his successor in the archdeaconry, and the residentiaries. 
t Canou of York 1404—9. See Test. Ebor. i. 853. 

t A very distinguished person, of whose history but little has been hitherto 
known. He takes bis name from Scarle, a village in Lincolnshire. 

In 1382 he was a clerk of the chancery of the higher grade. (Fots's Judges, iv. 
177.) In 1384 he was a clerk of parliament, and acted as such for many years, and 
in 1382 and for a long while afterwards, viz. in 1382-7, 1390.3, 1397 and 1399, he 
was a trier of petitions in parliament. (Rot. Pari., iii. var. toe.) On the 22nd of 
July, 1394, he was made master of the rolls, and held that office until Sept. 1396. 
(Newcourt, i. 340. Cal. Rot. Pat., 229. Dugd. Chron. 55.) As such, on August 
10th, 1397, he lent the king 200/. (Foodera, viii. 9), and on several occasions he bad 
tho temporary charge of the great seal. (Fobs, iv. 177.) From Sept. 1399, to March 
1401, Scarle was lord chancellor of England. (Ibid.) He continued to be a mem- 
ber of the king's council ; and in Jan. 1403, he and the bishop of Rochester were 
appointed to examine into tho evidences of the alien priories in England, it being 
recommended by the Commons that they should be resumed into the king's hand. 
(Acts and Ord. of the Privy Council, i. 190.) 

From 1382 to 1385 Scarle was vicar of Desborongh, Northants. (Bridges' North- 
ants, ii. 27.) On the 30th of October, 1385, he was instituted to the rectory of 
Althorp, co. Lincoln, which he held till 1390. (MSS. Cotton. Nero D. Hi. 239.) 
On the 13th of February, 1387-8, tho king gave him the stall of Ulleskelf at York. 
(Le Neve, iii. 219.) On the 11th of October, 1396, the abbat and convent of West- 
minster presented bim to tho rectory of St. Bride, London. (Newcourt, i. 316.) 
Ou the 27th of August, 1397. the chapter of York sent him to parliament as their 
proctor (Acta Cap. Ebor.). and on the 19th of September, 1400, he was collated to 
the stall of Weighton in that church. He seems also to have been vicar of Northall 
when he died (Newcourt, i. 702), and perhaps he waa sometime rector of St. Thomas 
at Winchelsea. (Cooper's Winchelsea, 141.) Between 1401 and 1403 ho was arch- 
deacon of Lincoln (Le Neve, ii. 45), and he was also rector for a while of Holme-by- 
tbe-Sea. (Blomefield's Norfolk, x. 833.) Scarle is said to have been buried in the 
church of St. Bride at London. (Willis, i. 177.)

* A son of Sir John Heron of Eppleden, oo. Durham, knight. His first wife was 
Elizabeth lady Say, and heiress of Thomas de Braosc, from whom (who died childless, 
July 8th, 185)9) her husband had assumed the title of Lord Say. He remarried Eli. 
zabeth, daughter of Thomas Boteler, lord Sudeley. 

Sir William died childless on the 80th of October, 1404. He saw much service 
abroad, and held many state employments. Henry IV., when he came to the throne, 
made him lord steward of the household, and in 1400 he was an ambassador to 
France. His will is in many respects a remarkable one. It is taken from the registry 
at Lambeth, and I am indebted for it to the kindness of the librarian. 

This notice of the testator is taken from a privately printed account of the family of 
Heron, drawn up by Sir R. Heron.

In 1391 be succeeded his father, and enjoyed the title for some fifteen years, dying on 
the 25th of January, 1406. He was a man of great wealth, for he was the owner of 
vast estates. His wife was Margery daughter of John Lord Welles, and widow of 
John Lord Huntingfield, and by her be bad a large family. (Scropo and Grosvenor 
Roll, ii. 130, etc.) 

He took bis title from Masham in Richtnondshire. His residence was at Clifton, a 
mile or two from Masham, on the banks of the Yore, and it was castellated.

would rest beside him. There is no more interesting place in the minster than thi*.

• A family long connected with Upsall, near Think. Several members of it were 
benefactors to Byland Abbey. (Burton's Monaaticon, 333, 335, &c.) On the 9th of 
December, 1349, the will of Sir Geoffrey de Upsall, knt. was proved, and adminis-

J Stephen le Scrope, the son of the testator, arose to some eminence in the Church 
through the influence of his uncle the archbishop. 

On March the 21st, 1395-6, whilst his uncle was bishop of Lichfield, he was collated 
to the prebend of Offley in that church, which he gave up in 1397 for that of Colwich. 
This he exchanged on 15th of June, 1400, for the stall of Dernford, which he resigned 
almost immediately. (Le Neve, i. 691, 596, 615.) 

On the 14th of May, 1400, be was appointed chancellor of the university of Cam- 
bridge, and he held the same office in 1414. (Le Neve, iii. 599.) On the 17th of Sep- 
tember in the latter year Henry IV. requested him to put an end to the quarrels be- 
tween the masters, regents, and non-regents, and the graduates and scholars in civil 
and canon law. (Fa?d. xii. 158.) 

In the year 1400 he was beneficed in the diocese of York, and a burst of preferment 
broke all at once upon him. Ou the 28th of December, 1399, he was collated to the 
stall of Langtoft at York (Reg. Scrope, 2 a), which he held for a twelvemonth. In 
February, 1399-1400, be was made prebendary of Knaresbro*, which he ceded in March 
1401-2. (Ibid.) On the 19th of May, 1400, the archbishop made him archdeacon of 
Richmond on the death of Thomas de Dalby (Ibid. 3 a) ; this honourable post, however, 
went for a short time to Nicholas de Bubwith by papal provision. On the 12th of 
June Scrope was ordained subdeacon, and deacon on the 18th of September. (Reg. 
Scrope.) On the 4 th of March, 1400-1 , the archbishop collated him to the stall of Drif- 
field, which he exchanged with Bubwith on the 18th for the archdeaconry of Rich- 
mond. (Reg. Scrope, 3 6, 9 a.) This was a pleasant way of evading the difficulty 
of the papal provision. On the 18th of October, 1401, Scrope, then domestic chaplain 
to his uncle, was made by him the prebendary of Studley at Ripon. (Reg. Scrope, 4 a.) 
This be held till Jan. 1408-9, when he exchanged it with Thomas de Polton for the 
stall of Knaresbro' at York. (Reg. Bowet, 40 a.) Scrope was a residentiary at York, 
and is always styled " junior " to distinguish him from bis father. 

On the 23rd of June, 1415, his ill-fated brother Henry lord Scrope left him in his 
will " unum par tabellarum cerearum de argento, deauratum ; et unum librum de 
Omeliis S. Gworgii ; et alium librum de Omcliis S. Remigii ; et alium librum de Ome- 
Iiis Yen. Bed® presbiteri ; et unum librum de Revelationibus S. Brigids Virginia, 
quem emi Beverlaci, pro remembrancia." (Feed. ix. 277.)

VIII. THE WILL OF SIR THOMAS NEVILLE, KNT., LORD 

PURNIVAL. 

[Hog. Dec. et Capit. Ebor. , sede vacanto, 315-16.] 

March 12, 1406-7. In nomine Sanctae et Individuae Trinitatis, 

• A place called Rocs Hall, in Water-Fulford, near York, belonged to the baronial 
house of Roos of Hatnelac and Belvoir. It was sold in the first of Queen Mary by 
Henry earl of Rutland to John Redeman, of Gate Fulford, gent 

John Roos, dean of the king's chapel, was prebendary of Masham, at York, in 
1395. A member of the house of Roos of Ingmanthorpe near Wetherby was also in 
orders about this time. 

t Rector of Wensley, to which he was instituted on the presentation of Sir Richard 
lo Scrope, April 4th, 1395. (MSS. Harl. 6978, 18a.) He was prehendary of South 
Muskham at Southwell. He resigned it on the last of February, 1396-7, and was 
re-admitted to it on the presentation of the king on the 8th of March. On the 24th 
of January, 1407, he was admitted to the stall of Dotevant at York, the king 
presenting him. On the 18th of October, 1409, the bishop of Durham collated him 
to the mastership of Grcatham Hospital. On the 20th of May, 1410, he was instituted 
to the prebend of Clifton at Lincoln ; and in the autumn of the same year he gave up 
his stall at Southwell. On the 24th of March, 1413-14, ho was made archdeacon of 
Huntingdon, and gave up bis prebend of Clifton. (Fasti Ebor. MSS.) 

Tibbay was chancellor of Joan the queen of Henry IV. (Coll. Topog. v. 282.) 
His end was a melancholy one, and Stowo shall describe it, " On Mary Magdalen day, 
in London, John Nicansor, esq., with nine of bis men, set upon and slew John Tibbay, 
clerk, archdeacon of Huntingdon, and chancellor to queen Joan. He and four of 
his men fled to St. Anne's church within Aldersgate, where they were mured up with 
boord, and watched day and night till the 21 of August ; on the which day they 
forsware the land, and passed through the cittie towards Calice in their shirts and 
breaches, each of them having a erase in his hand, and a purse about his necke." 

Hereby must hang a tale. John Niandoor, esq. was the husband of Margaret the 
widow of Roger lord Scrope of Bolton. Tibbay's connection with the Scropes was a 
close one. He was an executor not only of the testator, but of his father Richard 
lord Scrope, in 1400. (Test. Ebor. i. 278.) There must have been some feud or 
family quarrel. Tibbay was buried in St. Mary's chapel, within the monastery of the 
Grey Friars in London. His will is in existence.

On the 7th of November, 1379, he was admitted to the archdeaconry of Cleveland. 
(MSS. Cotton. Vitellius, A. II. 121a), and on the 18th he was admitted totheprecen- 
torsbip, exchanging Cleveland for it with Roger de Ripon. (Ibid.) On the 23rd of 
Jan. 1396-7, the chapter of York, whilst the see was vacant, made Kexby penancer 
(Reg., tede vacant*, 203 b), and, on tho 29th of May, 1409, he was made penancer 
in tho church of York. He is styled licentiate in theology. (Reg. Capit.) On 
the 14th of March, 1406-7, ho was appointed keeper of the" spiritualities of York 
during the vacancy of the see. (Reg., tede racante, 281 a.) His life seems to have 
had few incidents of importance in it. 

John dc Kexby, chancellor of York, was his nephew.

XI. THE WILL OF JOHN PROPnETE, DEAN OF YORK. 
[Reg. Test. Dec. et Cap. Ebor. i. 176.] 

London, April 8, 1416. Johannes Prophete,f decanus Ebor. 
— Corpus meum putridum tradendum ecclesiastical sepulturac infra 

* A merchant and goldsmith of York. Free 1386. Bailiff 1887-8. Lord Mayor 
1407, H08, and 1409. Died 5th August, 1419, and was buried at St. Crux. He 
married Agnes, daughter and co-heir of John de Barden, alderman of York. She 
died 22nd Sept. 1413. These dates are from a brass in the church of St. Crux ; 
those in print arc incorrect. For an interesting account of the Wymans see a notice 
of the indulgence cup of archbishop Scrope, published in the Archaeological Transac- 
tions, by R. Davies, F S.A. — R.I1.S. 

f John Prophete, dean of York, held a high position both in church and state. 

In 1389 and 1390 he occurs as clerk of the Privy Council. (Acts and Ord. of the 
Privy Council, i. 12, ice.) In the 6th of Henry IV. he occurs as the king's secretary 
(Cal. Rot. Pat. 250), and, soon afterwards, he became keeper of the privy seal, in which 
capacity he was appointed one of the executors of the king's will in 1 408. (Nichols's Royal 
Wills, 205; Cal. Rot. Pat. 259 ; Rot. Pari.) Many of his official letters as keeper 
of the privy seal are in MSS. Harl. No. 431. On the 12th of Nov. 1400, ho was 
employed in some negotiations connected with the restitution of queen Isabella (Faed. 
viii. 164), and on the 18th of October, 1414, he was appointed ambassador to 
ncgociatea marriage with Katherine of France. (Ibid. ix. 182.) In that year be was 
one of the executors of Beatrix lady Roos. (Test. Ebor. i. 378.) 

His ecclesiastical preferments were numerous. In 1382 be was rector of Adisbam 
in Kent. (Hasted, iii. 671.) This he exchanged on the 11th of May, 1386, with Wil- 
liam Lye, for the rectory of Haseley (MS8. Harl. 6952, 10a) ; and he again exchanged 
Hascley, on Dec. 2nd, with Raymond Pelegrim, for the prebend of Milton at Lincoln. 
(Ibid. 106.) He resigned this stall in 1405, when he was appointed to that of Leighton 
Buzzard, in the same church. (Le Neve, ii. 171.) On the 7th of November, 1393, he 
was installed dean of Hereford, holding that office until 1407; in which year he gave 
up the prebends of Moreton, Piona Parva, and Warham and Ayleston in the same 
church. (Le Neve, i. 476, 615, 522, 529.) 

On the 22nd of October, 1404, archbishop Scrope collated him to the stall of 
Langtoft at York. (MSS. Torre.) This he exchanged with Thomas de Waileworth 
for the prebend of Bugthorpe, to which he was admitted by the Chapter, during the

* A person about whom there is very little known. It is supposed that he was a 
member of the family of Strickland of Sizergb, but his connection with it has not 
been made out. (Nicolson and Burn, i. 94.) 

In 1395 the prior and convent of Carlisle chose him bishop, bat the pope pre* 
vented his election. (Le Neve, iii. 236.) In 1399, when bishop Marks was in dis- 
grace, Strickland was more successful. The pope provided him to Carlisle, and on 
the 15th of November the temporalities were restored to hin. (Food. viii. 106.) On 
Sunday, the feast of the Assumption of the Virgin (August 15th), 1400, he was con- 
secrated by archbishop Scrope in the chapel of Cawood castle, Louis bishop of Vol- 
terra, William bishop of Pharos, and John Shirburne abbat of Selby assisting him. 
(Reg. Scrope, 1516.) 

On the 9th of May, 1400, Bishop Strickland and Henry earl of Northumberland 
were ordered to arrest certain ecclesiastics who said that Richard II. was alive in 
Scotland. (Fad. viii. 255.) 

Bishop Strickland is said to have "built the tower and belfrey in the cathedral 
church, and to have furnished it with four bells, covering the pyramid on the tower 
with lead, and to have furnished the tabernacle work in the quire. He built the 
tower at Rose, which still goes by the name of Stirkland Tower. And he was at the 
expense of drawing a watercourse from the river Petterel through the town of Pen- 
rith, to the great benefit of the inhabitants. He likewise founded a chantry in the 
church of St. Andrew at Penrith. He died Aug. 30, 1419; and lies buried in 
the north isle of the cathedral, under his portraiture elegantly cut in plain stone." 
(Nicolson and Bum, ii. 272.) 

This will requires no remark.

square plate of brass." (Torre's York Minster, MS. 242.)

XV. THE WILL OP ROGER WHELPDALE, BISHOP OF CARLISLE. 

[Reg. archiep. Bowet, pan i. 287 a 

In Dei nomine, amen. Ego Rogerus, humilis minister, licet 
indignus, cathedralis ccclcsiae Karliolensis,* vicesimo quinto die 
Januarii, in die, videlicet, Conversions Sancti Pauli, Dei gratia 
solum confisus, corporaliter mentis compos, condo voluntatem 
mcam testimonialem in hunc modum. Profiteor primo sancta; 

• Bishop Whelpdale, who makes the following pious and characteristic disposition 
of his worldly effects, is said to have been a native of Cumberland. He wont to Ox- 
ford and became a fellow of Dalliol College. (Hist. Oxford Colleges, 85.) Afterwards lie 
was a fellow of Queen's (157), of which college he was made provost on the 15th of 
April, 1404 (146), the archbishop of York confirming his appointment on the 24th. 
(Reg. Scrope.) He resigned his office in 1420. He founded an eleemosynary chest 
in the college, to which he gave 36/. 16a. id. (Hist. Oxford Collogcs, 157.) In 1403 
Whclpdale was one of the proctors for the University. (Appendix, 36.) 

In 1412 Whelpdale was presented by tho bishop of Winchester to the living of 
Stockton in the diocese of Salisbury, which he resigned in the following year. 
(Phillipps' Wiltshire Incumbents, 102.) 

Whelpdale received the temporalities of the see of Carlisle on March 17th, 1419-20, 
and made his profession of obedience on August 1st. He died 4th Feb. 1422-3, and 
was buried in St. Paul's cathedral. (Le Neve, iii. 238. Nicolson and Burn, ii. 272.) 

Whelpdale is said to have written several treatises, particularly on mathematics and 
logic, which are mentioned in the usual text.books of literary biography.

In 1433 he became prebendary of Stow Longa, at Lincoln, and gave it up when ap-

XXIX. THE WILL OF^ WILLIAM FELTER, DEAN OP YORK. 

(Reg. Teat. Capit. Ebor. i. 267 a.) 

April 6, 1451. Willelmus Felter,* decanus Eboracensis.— 
sep. m eccl. cath. Ebor. Lego 1 li. ad usum ecclesiac, reponendas 

* William Felter, dean of York, seems to have been a native of Bristol. I am un- 
acquainted with his early history, but he was introduced to Yorkshire hy archbishop 
Kempe, whose chancellor he was. On Feb. 20th, 1429.30, the primate gave him the 
stall at St. Peter's altar at Beverley, which he resigned in Jan. 1450-1. (Reg. Kempe, 
8 b, 71 a.) On June 21st, 1435, he wa* collated to the archdeaconry of York (Ibid. 
15 6.), in which he was installed in person on July 7th. (Acta Capit. Ebor.) In 
December, 1436, Felter became dean of York. On the last day of Feb., 1441-2, he 
ww collated to the stall of Apesthorpe (Kempe, 47 a.), in which he was installed by 
proxy on 8th March, and in person on May 0th. (Acta Capit. Ebor.) On Jan. 14th, 
1450.1, he wa* collated to the stall of Driffield (Reg. K empe, 71 a-), and, on March 
15th, he was one of the persons appointed by the primate to act as his vicar-general. 
He was rector of Almond bury at bis death (Reg. Kempe, 74 ft.), and between 1407 
and 1485 he was dean of Wolverhampton. (MS8. Harl. 6952,66 *. Shaw's Stafford- 
shire, ii. 154.) 

On Feb. 5, 1435-6, Felter was one of the commissioners appointed to renew the 
truce between England and Scotland. (Foid. x. 629; Rot. ScotuB, ii. 294.) 

Felter died on the 10th of April, 1451, and was interred in the middle choir of 
York Minster, where an inscription in brass commemorated him. (Drake, 514.) He 
was a doctor of decrees. In 1454 his executors founded a chantry in the Minster at 
the altar of SS. Anne, Anthony, and Crux, for the dean's soul, and those of John and

* Nicholas Vicars, ** quondam vice-comes civitatis Ebor," who died 26th Jan. 
1488-9, is buried in the church of St. Michael, Ouse Bridge. His name does not 
occur in any of the printed lists of sheriffs, but I find from the city records that John 
Beverley, the senior sheriff, died in office, 17th July, 1st Henry VII. (1486) and that 
Nicholas Vicars, one of the chamberlains, was elected in his stead July 24th. Nicholas 
Vicars was a grocer, and was free in 1471 by purchase. His will bears date 21st 
January, 1488-9 He left a widow, Ellen, and a son, John.— R. H. S. 

Simon Vicars, of the parish of St. Michael, Ouse Bridge, chapman and haberdasher, 
was free in 1500; chamberlain, 1511 ; sheriff, 1513*14 ; lord mayor, 1521 (being 
elected in the room of Thomas Bank house, who died in office). Died at East 
Witton in Wensleydale in 1534, and was buried there. Will dated 22nd December, 
1534. (Prob. Jan. 12th, 1534-5.) By his first wife, who was buried at SL Michael's, 
he had a son, Simon, and two daughters, Agnes and Margaret. The hitter died 
unmarried in 1520. In her will, dated 24th Feb. 1619-20 (pr. 13th March), she 
desired to be buried in the above church, near her mother. She bequeathed property 
at Scarbro* and Palsgrave to her father, Simon Vicars, for his life, with remainder to 
her brother Simon. 

By his second wife (living 1519) alderman Simon Vicars had a son, Thomas, who 
was living in 1531.— R. H. 8.

XXXII. THE WILL AND INVENTORY OF MR. WILLIAM DUP- 
FIELD, CANON RESIDENTIARY OP YORK, SOUTHWELL, 
AND BEVERLEY. 

[Keg. Test. Capit Ebor. i. 272 et seq. et orig. Inv.j 

In festo Purif. B. M. V., 1452, Willelmus Duffeld * canonicus 
residentiarius in eccl. cath. Beati Petri Ebor., canonicusque eccl. 

• The testator, who wu a distinguished and very wealthy person, probably took 
his name from North or South Duffield, two villages to the sooth of York, a district 
with which from his will be seems to have been connected. 

In early life Duffleld went to Oxford, and in 1407, being a member of Merton col- 
lege, he was a proctor for the University. (Le Neve, iii. 480.) 

I find that William Duffield of York was ordained acolyte Feb. 19th, 1417-18; 
subdeacon March 12th, Trinity priory giving him a title ; deacon 21st May, 1418; 
and priest 11th March, 1418-19, — a very rapid progress. (Keg. Bowel.) 

On May 6th, 1421, the king collated him to a stall in the cathedral of Listens: 
(Feed. z. 112), and, on Oct. 27th, 1422, he was made rector of Copford in Essex. 
(Newcoort, ii. 192.) On the 23rd of March, 1425, he was installed archdeacon of 
Colchester, and he held that office until 1488. (Ibid. 189. Le Neve, il. 840.) 

Duffield held several very lucrative and important offices in the dioceao of York, 
through the kindness of archbishop Kempe. On March 22nd, 1428-9, he was col- 
lated by him to a stall at Beverley. (Reg. Kempe, 76.) On Sep. 17, 1432, the asms 
prelate sppointed him pretendary of Norwell O verbal 1 at Southwell. (Reg. Kempe, 
106.) This he resigned in Oct. 1450, but was re-appointed Nov. 7, 1451, and held 
that post till he died. On the 3rd of May, 1433, he was collated by the archbishop, 
whilst he was at Calais, to the stall of Wirtow at York (Kempe, 116) and, in Sept. 
1434. to the archdeaconry of Cleveland. (Ibid. 15a.) 

Duffield died, as appears from the title of bis inventory, on the 7th of March, 
1452-3 There is, however, no monument to commemorate him in York minster. 
He was a person of vast wealth, as may be seen from the inventory of his effects. 

Several persone of his name occur in the York registers, but I cannot weave a pedi- 
gree out of their wills. 

Die Martis p. f. S. Mat. Apostoli, 1390, Agnes, uxor Johannis Duffeld, pelliparii 
Ebor. To be buried in the church of St. Michael's, Ousebridge. IHughters Agnes 
and Ellen. Pr. 8 May. (Reg. Test. i. 23a.) 

June 15, 1394. Johannes de Duffeld de Ebor., pellipariua. — sep. in eccl. 8. Mi-

XXXIII. THE WILL OF MR. JOHN CASTELL, 8. T. P., PRECENTOR 
AND CANON-RESIDENTIARY OF YORK, AND RECTOR OF 
RUDBY. 

[Reg. Test. Capit. Ebor. i. 281.] 

In Dei nomine, amen. Ego Johannes Castell,* indignus 
sacerdos, ecclesiae sacrosanctas nlius poenitens, ac fidei catholics 
subditus humilisque professor, compos mentis et libera proprie-

* Tho beautiful and striking will of a York dignitary, Jobn Castell. 

On Sept. 23rd, 1402, a person of the name of John Castell was ordained subdeaoon 
at York, the monastery of St. Andrew giving him a title (Reg. Scrope), and he, being 
a master of arts, was made d<ncon Sept. 18, 1406, receiving his title from the hospital 
of St. John, without the east gate at Oxford. (Reg. Dec. et Cap. itdt vncante, 302 6.) 
In 1405 John Castell of Univ. Coll. was a proctor at Oxford. (Le Neve, iii. 480.) 
About 1413 he became master of Univ. Coll. (Ibid. iii. 537), and was made chancellor 
by patent dated April 17, 1422 (Ibid. iii. 467), and he held that office in 1425. (Hist. 
Univ. Oxon. v. 42.) In 1424 he was one of the executors of Ralph earl of Westmor- 
land. (Durham Wills, i. 73.) Ho was chaplain to Henry V. (Hist. Univ. Oxon. v. 
42.; Smith's Annals of Univ. Coll. 164.) 

On Nov. 15th, 1423, he was made chancellor of Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 93.) On 
Sept. 15th, 1431, he was collated to the archdeaconry of Berkshire (Ibid. ii. 635), and 
held it for a year. On Sept. 2nd, 1430, he was appointed to the golden stall at Hereford 
(Ibid. i. 501), having become chancellor there on July 7, 1425. (Ibid. i. 492 ) In 
1435 he resigned the stall of Carlton-cum-Kyme at Lincoln. (Ibid. ii. 121.) From 
1428 to 1430 he seems to have been rector of St. Clement Danes, London. (New- 
court, 1. 572.) 

In Yorkshire, on Oct 18, 1423, he was instituted to the rectory of Rudby on the 
death of Robert de Wyclsffe, which he held until his death (Reg. Bowet, i. 164 6); 
and, on Jan. 9, 1424-5, he was admitted to the stall of Skelton at Howden, which he 
resigned in 1436. (Reg. ude vacant*, 873 a.) On Feb. 12, 1435-6, he was admitted 
to the prebend of Wetwang and the rectory of Cottingham, exchanging for them with 
Nicholas Dixon his stall of Cheminster and Bere at Salisbury. (Reg. Kempe, 166.) 
On Oct. 7, 1447, he was appointed precentor. On June 12th, 1447, the archbishop 
appointed a commission to receive his resignation of the living of Cottingham, which 
he gave up owing to old age and infirmities, and a pension out of it was granted to 
him. (Ibid. 110 a.) 

Castell died in one of the early months of 1457, and was buried in York minster, 
and the following striking epitaph commemorated him. (Drake, 499.) It was near 
the font in the nave on " a broad white stone, about throe yards long, inscribed both 
on its verge and cross ways." (MS. Torre, 148.)

* Elizabeth Sy wardby, or Sewerby, as it is now called, was a daughter of Sir Henry 
Vavasour of Haalewood. (Test Ebor. ii. 162.3.) 8ome extracts from the will of her 
husband are given in Test. Ebor. ii. 136-7. Her only daughter, Margaret, married 
Sir Geoffrey Pigot, of Clotherham, near Ripon, and her will occurs afterwards. 

On Nov. 13, 1453, an oratory was granted to Geoffrey Pigot, of Sewerby, esq. and 
Margaret bis wife at Sewerby. (Reg. Win. Booth, 884a.) On Nov. 3rd, 1454, they 
had a similar licence. (Ibid. 8916.) On 12th Nov. 1455, the same favour was allowed 
to dame Eliz. Sy wardby, and Pigot and his wife. (Ibid. 895a.) Elizabeth Sy wardby, 
in her will, which has not been discovered, left the residue of her estate to maintain 
a regular chaplain at Sewerby, on account of its distance from Bridlington. (Beg. 
Geo. Neville, i. 102.) 

This Inventory was drawn up on the 30th of April, 1468, by Robert Scathlott, Jobs 
King, and Thomas Wells, citizens of York.

* An ecclesiastic who held high offices in the diocese of York and made a pious 
disposition of his wealth. 

On May 19th, 1435, Mr. John Lathum was instituted to the rectory of Knecsall, 
Notts, at the presentation of Norton Abbey (Reg. arch. Kemp, 381 6.) ; and, on Deo. 
17, he was ordained acolyte on that title. (Ibid. 260 a.) On July 15th, 1443, he was 
instituted to the rectory of Thorner, on the king's presentation (Ibid. 50 a.), and on 
May 22nd, 1445, he was ordained priest, being then dean of the royal chapel in 
Pootefract Castle. (Ibid. 282 a.) On Feb. 16th, 1447-8, he was admitted to the 
perpetual chantry in the college of the Holy Trinity at Pootefract called Knolles 
Almshouses ; and, on the 10th of May following, he was instituted to the mastership 
of the said college, the priory of Nostell presenting him. (Ibid. 411 a.) On Jan. 28th, 
1450-1, Lathum, being secretary to the archbishop, was collated by him to the prebend 
at St. Peter's altar in Beverley minster. (Ibid. 71 a.) 

In 1444 we find Lathum receiving a very considerable pension. On the 24th of 
April In that year John, prior of the house of St. Robert at Knaresbro' was at Cawod 
castle, and there, in a high chapel or oratory, on the south side of the principal 
chamber there, the prior put in Lathum'a hands a deed of gift, making over to him an 
annual pension of 23 1. 6 #. 8 d. an immeuse sum for that poverty-stricken house to 
bestow. (Reg. Kempe, 1H66.) 

On Jan. 27, 1446-7, Lathum was instituted to the rectory of Betham, St. Mary's 
Abbey, York, presenting him ; but he resigned it in the following month. (Reg. 
archid. Richmond, 10 a.) In May, 1469, be became rector of Aldford in Cheshire. 
(Ormerod's Cheshire, ii. 414.) 

Lathum was a member of the great Lancashire family of that name and ilk, and my 
Lancashire friends will thank me for the genealogical notices which this will contains.

X There is nothing in print relating to the family of Ferriby, and I shall not 
attempt here to supply the deficiency. Many members of it were connected with the 
church of York, and some of them held high offices in the state. A pedigree of them 
may be constructed. 

Ferriby seems to have been one of the valets of the crown. (Reg. Test. ii. 595.) 
His will is curiously original. He married Margaret, widow of Thomas Roos. e«q. 
of Routh in Holderneas. A license to unite them was directed on Dec 13th, 1463, 
to John Gisburgk, canon residentiary of York, Mr. Thomas Gedney, and Mr. Thomas 
Bentley. (Reg. Will. Boothe, 220 a.) On Oct. 14, 1465, John Ferriby, and Marga. 
ret bis wife, were allowed to have an oratory. (Reg. Geo. Neville, i. 51 a.)

Oxford, and being a favourite in that office the University wrote to the pope to ask

On 29th May, 1445. Sever was collated to the stall of Harleston at St. Paul's, which 
be held till he died in 1471 (Newcourt, i. 153), and on the 28th April, 1449, he was 
made chancellor of the same church, an office which his death vacated. (Ibid. i. 113.) 
From 1455 to 1471 he was warden of Merton College, having been proctor in 1427. 
(Wood, iv. 7.) He did so much for his college in building, etc. that he was almost 
regarded as a second founder. In Uic chapel " near to the entrance into the choir, on 
the right hand, is a very fair marble stone, with the picture of a man from head to foot, 
cut on a large plate of brass, with canonical robes, and the facing thereof wrought with 
saints' figures."

as a reward for his skill, he was made bishop of Durham and just missed the cardina- 
late. I will only mention the preferments which be held in Yorkshire. On March 
18th, 1444.5, John Sherwood of York, B.A. bad letters diroissory to enable him to 
be ordained by any bishop. (Reg. Kempe 9Gb.) On July 9th, 1455, he was instituted

Sherwood was high in tho favour of archbishop Neville. He came from Cambridge 
and was incorporated M.A. and B.D. at Oxford, whilst Neville was chancellor there, 
on Oct. 29th, 1456. (Churton's Lives of the founders of Brasenoee, 299.) After thin, 
tbe two were intimately connected. Sherwood became the archbishop's chaplain, and 
drew up for his amusement, when be was ill, an epitome " de Ludo arithmomachtae," 
a singular specific for archiepiscopal complaints. This book was printed, and is 
exceedingly rare. 

I cannot make out the connection between the bishop and William Sherwood, dean

ham, iii, 334. Churton's Lives of the founders of Brasonose college, 299.) He died at 
Rome on Oct 11th, 1497, and was buried in the English Chapel there, near bishop 
Shorwood, where there is a monument to commemorate him. (Colk Top. et Genea)., 
v. 88.)

•f A will which gives me an opportunity of saying something about the history of a 
family which, notwithstanding its high position, is involved hi no little obscurity. 
The chief residence of the E urea was at Witton Castle in the county of Durham. 
They were a race of gallant soldiers and were famous among the Northern chivalry. 

On Sept. 9th, 1422, the will of Sir Ralph Euro knt. was proved before the bishop of 
Durham at Stockton, and administration was granted to Sir William Eure, knt. and 
Robert Eure, esq. bis sons and cxeoutors. (Reg. Langley, 113 6.) This was the grand- 
father of the testator.

widow of Sir William Eure, knt., is printed in Test Ebor. ii. 284-6. She died in 
1467 and desires to be buried in Malton abbey near her husband. In her will she 
mentions the testator. 

Old Malton, tiie residence of the testator, came to his grandfather, or perhaps great- 
grandfather, Sir Ralph Eure knt., by his marriage with Catherine, one of the co-heirs of 
Sir William do Ayton. By deed dated at Ayton on Michaelmas day, 1385, Sir 
William de Ayton, knt. conveyed to Sir Ralph Eure, Sir John Conyers, and Sir 
William Place, knta. his manor of Bardelby on Holme co. York, for their lives, with 
remainder to the heirs of the said Sir Ralph and Catharine hia wife, the heirs of Sir 
William do Place, knt., son of Sir William de Place, knt. deceased, and those of 
Elizabeth his mother, now wife of Sir John Conyers. (MSS. Harl. ecxlv. 128 b.) 

Old Malton, a portion of the old inheritance of the Veacies .whom the Aytons repre-

Cambridge, and for the support that he received from bishop Alcock.

1456, John Pakenham was admitted to the vicarage of Clavering-eum-Langley in 
the diocese of London, but was deprived in the course of the next year. (Newcourt, 
U. 155.) In 1459, Oct. 31st, he was instituted to the rectory of Tichmarsh, Northants, 
on the presentation of Hugh Pakenham, which be held till 1465. (Bridges'' Northants, 
ii. 385.) In 1460 he resigned the rectory of Lidiard Milicent in Wiltshire. 

John Pakenham died on Oct. 11th, 1477, and was buried in the nave of York 
Minster under "a blue marble stone, about four yards long, having the four Evan, 
gelists in as many caterfoyls at corners. In the midst this esoocheon quartered, viz: 
1st and last, gules and or, in the first quarter a cressant arg. 2nd and 3rd, threo 
cronells (of a spear) sable. Above it, a square plate bearing the inscription." (Torre s 
York Minster, MS. 171.) Pakenham was a benefactor to the Minster, giving to it, 
in particular, several pieces of hangings on which his arms were embroidered. 
(Fabric Rolls. 227-8, 231, 306. The Plumpton Correspondence. 261-2.) His will 
exhibits the painful spectacle of a man perplexed and overborne with debt. 

In the Plumpton Correspondence (14-15) there is a letter from Hugh 'Pakenham 
to Sir William Plumpton, dated at London on June 21st, 1465, in which he mentions 
his brother the treasurer of York, and says that "your dayly bede- woman, my 
buswif, desired she may humblie be recommended to your most loving mastership, 
and to signifie how God bred her to be delivered of her son Nicholas on Tewsday the 
4 of this month, and how that on Saturday last was my daughter Agnes accepted 
into the habitt of St. Dominike ordre att Dertford." 

It seems probable that the brothers were members of a Kent family, and that they 
were connected with archbiahnp Kempe. A Hugh Pakenham was sometime prebendary 
of Langtoft at York, and South Muskham at .Southwell, as well as rector of Hethara. 
If he is identical with the writer of the above-mentioned letter, it is evident that 
archbishop Kempe had bestowed some of his preferment upon a layman. This is the 
person who in 1411 occurs as an officer of that primate at Ripon, and was concerned 
in gathering the tolls when some disturbance was expected from the lads of Knares- 
borough forest. He prevented any serious riot by garrisoning the town with 200 
men from Hexhamshire, rough and wild fellows, who went " robling up the said 
towne and downe, saying, * Would God these knaves and lads of the forest would 
come hidcr that we might have a faire day upon them.*" (Preface to the Plumpton 
Correspondence, lv.)

1st, 1450, he was adm. to the fifth prebend at Leicester; and to the tint on Doc. 20th, 
1472. (Nichols's Leicestershire, i. 338.) In 1451 he was installed prebendary of

In the diocese of York Andrew held several pieces of preferment. On Nov. 29th, 
1445, archbishop Kempe collated him to the stall of Wartbill at York. (Reg. Kempe, 
56 b.) This he gave up when he was collated to the prebend of North Newbald on 
August 19th, 1449. (Ibid. 66 A.) On July 28th, 1461, he exchanged his prebend 
of Fontenell at ShafUbury witfi Andrew Holes, for one of tho stalls of Oxton-cum- 
Crophill at Southwell. (Reg. Will. Booth, 53 a.) This he resigned on Nov. 10th, 
1476, receiving a retiring ponsion of 20 marks per ann. Thrice— on June 8th, 1465; 
March 2nd, 1474-5; and June 8th, 1475. he was made vicar-general. 

In 1451 William Keller, dean of York, died, and Andrew was forced upon the 
chapter as his successor. That body selected their treasurer John Berningham, and 
a long and painful struggle ensued, which resulted in the Minster being put under 
an interdict. Thomas Uaaooigne boldly charges Andrew with carrying his point by 
bribery, but he was not formally installed as dean until the 1st of June, 1454. An 
account of the affair is to be found in the appendix to Hearne's edition of Walter of 
Heminghurgh, ii. 522. Andrew held the office of dean for many yean, and resigned 
it shortly before his death on July 8th, 1477. 

In 1443 Andrew was made secretary to Henry VI. I say nothing here of the 
many services that he rendered to the state, or of the embassies on which he was 
sent.

his life. (Orig. at Belvoir castle.) To this document the seal of the college is attached, 
and I am not aware that there is any other impression of it in existence. It is oval. 
Within a tabernacle the Virgin and Child are represented sitting. An old man, 
probably the earl, is on bis knees before them. In the corner are a king and a bishop. 
Above all, the Deity is depicted, looking down from a cloud. Below the tabernacle 
are the arms of Neville, supported in the most beautiful manner by two greyhounds, 
the heads of which are hidden under the flat base of the tabernacle above them. 
The inscription is injured. 

A more beautiful specimen of sigillary art it is difficult to conceive. The great earl 
seem to have been passionately fond of greyhounds. The skull of one was found, when 
his tomb was opened in Staindrop church, resting beside his lord.

On July 20th, 1479, the adm. of Joan Neville of York was granted to John Glatjn 
alderman of York and Joan his wife. (Reg. Test. v. 143 a.) This was, possibly, the

The testator, after he made his will and before his death, is said to have been 
knighted at Hutton-Moor by Richard duke of Gloucester in 1482. (Surtees, iv. 163.) 
It is evident that this was the case, as, on Oct. 24th, 2nd Kic. III. there is an order 
from that king for the officers, etc., of Thomtonbridge, Cundall, Letby, Norton, Kirkby- 
super-Moram, Humborton, ( ?) and 8ypton ( ?) within the county of York, and of the 
lordship of Carlbury, and Uinaby and Ingleton in the bishoprick of Durham, to pay 
their rents to dame Alice Neville for her life. (MSS. Harl. cccc.xxxiii. 193.) 

* The founder of the family of Witham of Cliffc, and Lartington in the North 
Riding of Yorkshire. He is said to have bee* a son of Robert Witham of Grantham, 
but, as to the truth of this statement, some further evidence is required. He comes 
before us, however, as the novus homo of a good old Yorkshire house, and it was 
through his influence and industry that its wealth and position were mainly secured. 
Witham was probably connected in early life with the family of Neville, and he was 
executor of the earl of Salisbury and his son the king-maker. (Test. Ebor. ii. 240, 
246.) On March 16th, 1471*2, ho was made a commissioner to treat with Scotland. 
(Focd. xi. 748.) He was also concerned with the affairs of that country in 1473. 
(Ibid. 776, 786.) Witkam's connection with the dominant family of the day made 
him employed more or less in public duties, and it will be found that he had fast 
friends in the lords Salisbury and Warwick, and in Richard duke of Gloucester, after- 
wards Richard III. From the windows of his hall at Cornburgh, he could look up 
to the stately towers of Sheriffhutton castle, which almost overshadowed his humbler 
residence. He was thus in constant connexion with one of the principal residences 
of the noble house of Neville, which had befriended him for so many years, and which 
be had served so faithfully and so well. 

The chief distinction of Witham 'a life was his holding the office of Chancellor of 
the Exchequer. He was thrice appointed to it by letters patent : 1st in 32nd Henry 
VI ; again in 34th Henry VI; and, lastly, in the 4th of Edward IV. On the second 
occasion ho was appointed for life. (Cal. Rot. Pat. 296, 297, 307.) He would acquire 
this honour through the influence of the Nevilles. 

t In a chantry-chapel in the north aisle of the church of Sheriffhutton, lies a blue 
marble slab with four small tablets for brasses, which have now disappeared. In the 
centre is the following inscription on a brass plate: 

Vestibulum fieri qui fecit, et ista capellam, 

Hie cantariam sistere perpetuam 
Fundans. Christe Thonuo Wytham miserere, suscquo 
Agnetis sponsse, qui simul hie recubant. 

The eaglets or sheldrakes in the arms of the Withams, are, I believe, merely the 
popinjays of the Thwengs. They are represented in brass in Sheriffhutton as 
debruised by a bendlct. I cannot speak here of this most interesting church, and the 
sepulchral memorials which it contains.

Sir John was high .sheriff of Yorkshire in 1455 and 1461, and M.P. for Yorkshire 
29th Henry VI. By Alice, daughter of Sir William Qascoigne, of Gawthorpe, he left 
a numerous family. He was chief-steward of the manor of Wakefield, and died at

through Wakefield, and was sumptuously interred at Thornhill. (Hunter's Notices of 
Lupaet, etc., 17.)

widow of Sir John Saville. ( Reg. Rotherham, 23 b.) On Jan. 14, 1493-4, Sir John 
Waterton, knt., administered to the effects of lady Saville and Elizabeth widow of 
Thomas Saville (Ibid. 361 b.) 

Sir John Saville in his will, in addition to the extracts that I have given, makes 
the following disposition of his estates. To Alice, his wife, his capital messuage of 
Coldby, etc., in the Isle of Axholme, and his lands at Estrington and Thurlestone in 
the parish of Penistone ; and, for her life, the manor and lands of Thornhill, and 
lands, etc., in Ovenden, Wadsworth and Skircotea, which Sir William Qascoigne and 
others gave them on July 1st, 28th Henry VI. To Henry, Richard, and Nicholas, 
his sons, each an annual rent-charge of 4/. out of the manor of Hunsworth. His 
feoffees to make over to William Saville, his son, half of the manor of Hunsworth, to 
him and hU heirs male — remainder to Thomas Saville his brother and his heirs male- 
remainder to testator's right heirs. The other moiety to go to Thomas, the testator** son 
and his heirs male; failing them, to William his brother and his heirs male; and, 
(ailing them, to the testator's right heirs.

* The bead of a family of great influence in Norfolk and in the West Riding of 
Yorkshire. Sir Hugh was the son of John Hustings of Fen wick by Anne daughter of 
lord Morley, and was a person potent in wealth and position. The chief estates of 
his house were in Norfolk ; but he had broad acres, as it will be seen, in Yorkshire.

Hastings nod Mary widow of Thomas Salvin, who were related in the 3rd and 4th

stock, and was widow of Thomas Salvin, esq., of Newbiggin. Richard III. made 
Hastings guardian of Sal fin's lands and of his son and heir. He also mado him

829.) 

Another brother, probably, was Sir Roger Hastings who sold the estate of Roxby in

culties. (Plumpton Correspondence, cxiii. 267.) On June 26th, 1484, the rector of

J Henry Gillow was one of the natives of Lancashire who came into Yorkshire 
with the archbishops Booth, and benefited largely by the migration. The family of 
Gillow is one of considerable antiquity. From 1466 to 1476 Henry Gillow was 
temporal chancellor of Durham. (MSS. Surtees.) Between 1470 and his death, he 
was rector of Houghton- le-Spring in that diocese (Surtees, i. 157), and, as rector, he 
seems to have given some trouble to the monks of Finchale in demanding tithe for 
coal at Finchale and Rainton. (Finchale Priory, 37-9.) It is possible that he is the 
same person who was presented, on May 21st, 1451, to the rectory of Stock in Pe) ham 
in the diocese of London. (Newcourt, i. 856.) Gillow was also master of Kcpyer 
hospital near Durham, which be resigned in 1479. (8nrtees, iv. part ii. 65.) 

On July 24th, 1476, Gillow was installed prebendary of Tockerington at York, on 
the presentation of archbishop Laurence Booth. (Reg. Cspit. Ehor.1 He exchange! 
this for Fridaythorpe, to which he was collated on* June 11th, 1479. (Reg. Lour. 
Booth, 7 a b.) On March 5th, 1477-8, he was installed eub-dean of York. (Regg. 
Capit. et Laur. Booth, 5 a, etc.) This he held until his death, together with the rectory 
of Gilling, in which he was installed July 13th, 1480. (Reg. udt vacante, 495 a.) 

On Dec. 31st, 1473, Robert Gillow, vicar-choral, was adm. to the chantry at St. 
Stephen's altar in York Minster for the soul of John Alkbarrow. (Reg. Capit.) On

letters dimissory; and priest on 17th March seq. (Reg. Rolherham.) March 12,

a stipend of 60s. per ann. (Orig. patent in tbe Auditor's office at Durham.) On Nov.

With the successors of archbishop Kempe at York, Bird was equally in favour. He 
was chaplain of archbishop William Booth. On Oct. 26th, 1457, that prelate gave 
him, "intuitu caritatis," the stall of Northwell at Southwell (Reg. 43a), which he

the stall of Fridaythorpe at York; which he gave up when promoted to that of 
Tockerington in the same church on June 11th, 1479. (Reg. Laur. Booth, 7 a.) 

In the diocese of London, Bird found a patron in the bishop, Thomas Kempe, 
nephew of the archbishop of York. He was by him made rector of Wideford on 
April 29th, 1454 (Newcourt, i. 908); rector of ChigweU May 12th, 1460 (Ibid. ii. 
142); and prebendary of St. Pancras at London, May 8th, 1470, which ho gave up 
for tbe stall of Islington, of which he became the tenant on March 31st, 1478. This 
he resigned in 1482. (Ibid. i. 168, 195.) 

Torre says that on the south side of the nave in the minster, " lyes a narrow blue 
stone, about two yards and a half long, rosed at corners, and bad in the midst the 
picture of a clergyman, with certain escrow lea about him bearing these words : 
*' Jesu, fili Dei, miserere tui Ranulphi, 
Dignatus cs nasci, miserere tui Ranulphi." 

Torre supposes that the stone is a memorial of Ranulph Bird. (MS. account of York 
Minster, 147.) This can scarcely be, as Bird desired to be interred close to the door 
of the chapel of the Blessed Virgin and the Holy Angels, which was on the other side 
of the nave. Close to the door of that chapel is the tomb, inserted in the wall, 
ascribed by some to archbishop Roger, but quite incorrectly. May not this be that of 
Bird ? The architecture, till restored, was of his time, and in the centre of the arch 
are two birds. The tomb was opened some time ago, and fragments of vestments were 
discovered, which are said to be of a very early date. This proves nothing, as the 
deceased would not be buried in a new vestment.

The testator, and many of his legatees, descend from Christopher Conyers, esq. of 
Hornby in Ricbmondshire. I am indebted to my friend Mr. Hailstone for some 
extracts from his will (hitherto unknown) which I made from a copy of it in his 
possession. 

" I Christofre Conyers, in hale minde. the Wedensday next after feast of St. Hillary 
the yhere 1426 — to be buryed in the kirk of Hornby beside my fader's toumbe, whose 
saule God assoyle ; beseking myn executors that they make nane enterement for me, nor 
other costage hot that is resonable and fitt for to be done upon my berying. To Rlene 
my wife, if she overlyve me, the third part of my godos. To John, my sonne, xl marc. 
100 marc for my saule, in finding of three prests and in alraous dedes. Johan and — 
my daughters. My wife enciente. To my son Thomas and his heirs my purchased 
lands, etc., in Hornby, Brokebolme, North Ottrington, and half of my purchased lands in 
Erythorne, Hunton, Heailton,and Little Crakehall, and the half of my lands in Whitby. 
John, now mine eldest son, under 21. My mother dame Margaret Conyers, John 
Pigot, and Richard Welden, exrs." 

The rector of Rudby was one of the younger children of Christopher Conyers, and 
was amply provided for in his will. He took orders somewhat late in life, and proba- 
bly with a view of being presented to the living of Rudby. On the 20th of Sept. 
1455, Cbr. Conyers of Hornby was made acolyte; subdeacon on 20 Dec., receiving 
bis title from Easby abbey ; deacon on Feb. 21 ; and priest on 18th March, seq., all 
within seven months. (Reg. Will. Booth.) On the last day but one of February, 
1456*7, be was instituted to the rectory of Rudby in Cleveland, on the presentation of 
Sir John Conyers, knt., his brother. This living he held till he died in the autumn of 
1483. (Reg. Will. Booth, 65 6.) In 1469 he was made a brother of the Corpus 
Christi guild at York. (MSS. Lansdowne, cccc.iii, 58 a.) On the 2$rd of November. 
1468, archbishop Neville allowed to Chr. Conyers the use of an oratory for a year. 
(Reg. i. lU7a.) 

The testator was evidently a person of wealth and piety. It will be seen that the 
will of his father proves the affinity of the family of Conyers of Whitby to that of 
Hornby.

thorpe in Cleveland, an estate which passed with an heiress, in the sixteenth century, 
to Geoffrey Lee of Delme Magna in Kent, and his descendants. This Brian Conyers, 
ia said by Wriothesley to have married Elizabeth, dau. of Thomas Nelson. 

On Oct. 5, 1478, Brian Conyers of York, merchant, made his will, which was 
proved on the 16th. He desired to be buried in the church of the Blessed Trinity in 
the King's Court. To Margaret (Nelson ?), his mother, he gave 68*. id. The residue 
was left to Elisabeth, his wife, and his children. (Reg. Test. v. 1306.) 

Another brother was Henry, who is said in MSS. Harl. 1540, to have died a. p. 
Possibly he was in orders. I find that Henry Conyers, of Hornby, was made acolyte 
on Dec. 17, 1457; aubdeacon, with a title from Eaaby Abbey, on 1st April; and priest 
on Sep. 23rd, 1468. (Reg Will. Booth.) 

Henry Conyers, the beginner of the line at Holtby, seems to have been an illegi- 
timate son. It is marvellous to see how all the brothers prospered in the world, but 
they were the sons of an illustrious and truly noble house.

CXXIV. THE WILL OF HENRY PERCY, EARL OP 
NORTHUMBERLAND. 

[Reg. Rotherbam, 347 b. tt W79.] 

In Dei nomine, amen. To the pleasure of Allmyghtie God, 
our Lady Saynte Marye the Virgyne, and all the Sayntes of 
heven and undir, and w l the suffrage of all holy church, I Henrie 
Percy,* crle of Northumbrelande, beyug in good helth and hole 

• The series of wills in this volume may terminate, very appropriately, with that of 
the head of the princely house of Percy. My readers will find an account of him in the 
Peerages ; and the document, which is now for the first time printed, is an interesting 
addition to the materials for his life. The great earl died in 1489, and was interred at 
Beverley with sumptuous magnificence. A noble monument still commemorates bim 
at the east end of that beautiful minster. 

The earl was murdered at Cox-lodge, near Thirsk, on the day of St. Vitalis. 1489, 
by a rabble he had affronted by his zeal in pressing the payment of an obnoxious tax. 
The laureate of the day thus commemorated his fall : 

He was environd about on every syde 

With his enemyes. that wer starke mad and wode : 

Yet while he stode he gave them woundes wyde : 
Alias for ruth ! what thoughe his myi.de wer gode. 
His co rage manly, yet ther he shed his blodc : 

Al left alone, alas, he fougbte in vayne ! 

For cruelly among tbem ther he was slayne. 

Alas for pite! that Percy thus was spylt, 

The famous Erie of Northumberland ; 
Of knyghtly prowes the sword, pomel, and hylt, 

The myghty lyon doutted by sc and land; 

O dolora* rhaunce of fortunes fro ward haude ! 
What man, remembryng howe shamfully he was slaine, 

From hitter weping him*elf can restrain ?

DISPENSATIONS FOR MARRIAGE, MARRIAGE 

LICENCES, ETC. 



I now give a list of all the licences and dispensations for mar- 
riage, ana the names of all the widows who took the vow of 
chastity, which appear in the registers of the archbishops of York, 
the bishops of Durham, and the archdeacons of Richmond. They 
arc arranged in chronological order, beginning with the reign of 
Richard II.; prior to which time there are few, if any, to be 
found. This series covers the whole tract of country from the 
H umber to the Tweed, and the information which it affords is 
novel and valuable, not only to the genealogist, but also to the 
ecclesiastical antiquary. A few words on each class of documents 
brought before my readers may be of some use. 

I. Marriage Licences. Marriages usually were celebrated after 
banns in the parish church of one of the two parties. Special 
leave, however, was necessary, if the two persons were to be 
married in a strange church; or if the banns were to be asked 
twice, or only once. Sometimes they were asked thrice on the 
same day, for the sake of expedition. Leave, also, was necessary, 
if the marringe was to take place in a private chapel or oratory. 
In that case, the incumbent of the parish was desired to allow it, 
and the banns were previously asked in the parish church. 

II. Dispensations. If two persons desiring to marry were re- 
lated to each other in the third or fourth degree of consanguinity ; 
if one of the two had been sponsor to the other, or a child of the 
other, they could not marry without a dispensation, and this was 
to be obtained in the pupal court. There were other connections 
also which rendered an alliance unlawful. Supposing that they 
had married in ignorance of the tie between them, the marriage 
was illegal, and the issue of it illegitimate. This also could be 
remedied by an ex post facto dispensation. The dispensation was 
issued on this wise. The p ope, or some member of the Sacred 
College acting in his behalf, listened to the case of the claimant, 
and, if it was proper, granted a dispensation legitimatising the 
marriage, past or future. This document, however, was not a 
final one. It was only to stand good in case that, after due exa- 
mination into the allegations contained in the petition by the 



Digitized by Google 



312 



TESTAMENTA E BOH AC EN SI A* 



bishop or archbishop at home, they were found to be correct, 
and in case that no improper influence had been brought to 
bear upon the woman to compel her to join in the petition. When 
the petitioner or his dispensation reached England, it was pre- 
sented to the prelate; and he, or his deputy, examined into the 
whole matter; and, if the statements of the petitioner were found 
to be correct, the dispensation took effect at once, and was 
entered in the prelate's register, and issued with the addition of 
his formal approval. In this examination the pedigrees of the 
two persons would be produced; and, on one or two occasions, 
they are entered on the register. It appears, also, that forged 
dispensations were sometimes offered and made use of by the 
unwary recipients. In the case of the marriage of Sir Henry 
Scrope and Philippa Ros in 1398, I have printed the papal 
dispensation, and the other formal documents connected with it, 
as a specimen of the class. Occasionally, I believe, English 
bishops had authority from the pope to grant these dispensations 
without an immediate reference to the papal court. Thomas 
Langley, bishop of Durham, was allowed to do so in twelve 
cases. 

III. Vows of Chastity. A lady, after her husband's death, 
was allowed to take the vow of chastity, and she was then called 
a vowess. A kind of investiture took place, generally, I believe, 
during or before the celebration of mass, when the officiator 
gave the vowess a pall or mantle, a veil, and a ring, and she 
then made a vow of chastity in a set form of words. The cele- 
brant was not necessarily a Bishop, but an Abbat or a Prior 
might act in his stead. This vow merely obliged the lady to 
live in chastity. She was not severed from the world, but could 
live in it and make a will, and dispose of her property as she 
chose. We sometimes find that the vowess, for the sake of a 
stricter and a more retired life, took up her abode in or near 
some monastery, particularly a nunnery. She was, however, 
merely a lodger, or, to use the old term, a perheiidinaria. I have 
given many examples of the vows that were taken by these 
ladies. The whole subject opens out a new phase of mediaeval 
life.

THE SURTEES SOCIETY. 



REPORT FOR THE YEAR MD.CCC.LXIV. 

[food at At General Meeting on tkt 7ih qf June]. 

Thirty years have passed away since the Surtees Society was 
founded, and the members may well congratulate themselves 
on the position that it at present occupies. There are ups and 
downs in the history of every literary association ; there are 
times when workers become weary and supporters listless ; and 
then there is a crisis full of peril and discouragement, which 
is too often fatal in its consequences. The Surtees Society is 
not unacquainted with these dangers, but it has had the good 
fortune to be uninjured by them. Not only has it the gratifi- 
cation of being the oldest of the English Societies, but it has 
also the pride of feeling that, after tliirty years spent in hard 
and honest work, it is still full of life and energy, eager to 
devise new plans and schemes, and anxious to carry them out 

During the past year there have been twelve vacancies in 
the list of members, but this loss has been more than compen- 
sated for by the election of thirty-eight new associates. Tin's 
is a most gratifying increase in our numbers, and yet it is not 
above the average of the last five or six years. Ten years ago 
we had only one hundred and fifty members, now we have as 
many as three hundred and thirty; and by a resolution passed 
at our last general meeting it was resolved that the number of 
associates should be limited to three hundred and fifty. By 
taking this step the Society hopes to attain and keep a fixed 
and steady basis on which it can work, without being either 
lead astray by ambition, or thwarted and dismayed by poverty. 

Not only have the additions to our list of members been so 
great, but the balance-sheet of the Treasurer is very decidedly 
in favour of the Society. The sale of the publications is large, 
and the more recent volumes have been speedily out of print 



Digitized by Google 



2 



This has induced the Council to raise, in many instances, the 
prices of the volumes to non-subscribers. The Council 
has no wish to afford facilities for purchasing them to the 
injury of the members; and, in the present condition of the 
Soeictv, every one must see that it will be very much to his 
interest to secure our publications as a subscriber and not as 
a stranger. 

The Council is fully conscious that the chief reason for the 
great prosperity of the Society at the present time is the largo 
and increasing support which it receives from the gentlemen 
of Yorkshire. From the fact that about half of the members 
of tho Society are Yorkshiremen, the Council is rejoiced to 
sec that not only are its Yorkshire works (published and pro- 
posed) properly appreciated, but, also, that its position as the 
literary association for that great county is fully recognised 
and understood. The Society will now be able to take in hand 
more Yorkshire subjects than it has hitherto been able to do ; 
but it must still be remembered that there are other districts 
which liave just claims upon its attention which cannot bo 
passed over. 

There has, we are sorry to say, been a considerable delay in 
the issue of the publications of the Society for several years, 
but tho nature of tho subjects that have been taken in hand 
renders this delay unavoidable. No one can have any concep- 
tion of the toil and tho research that are necessary to prepare 
anything in the shape of a chronicle for the press ; and every 
allowance ought to be made for an editor who is disposed to 
edit one with the care that it deserves. Tho labour and the 
ex]>ense of doing so are necessarily considerable; and nothing 
save a love for his subject and a true interest in the welfare 
and the reputation of the Society, can induce any one to take 
upon himself so great a burden. The kind forbearance that 
has l>een manifested by the members of the Society is a proof 
that they appreciate and are grateful for the labours of their 
ed iters. 

There aro two works in progress for the current year. 

Tho first is a third volume of Wills from the Registry at 
York, a series of very great interest. This volume will pro- 
bably end at tho beginning of the reign of Henry VIII., and 
those who aro conversant with the valuable documents which 
have been already drawn from that rejxwitory, will look for- 
ward with eager interest to a continuation of them. Some 
early Inventories, also, have been discovered, and will bo pub- 
lished ; including those of two Archbishops of York in the 



Digitized by Go 



3 



fifteenth century. The value of the pictures of domestic life 
which these documents reveal to us cannot be over-estimated. 

The second is the concluding volumo of the Memorials of 
the Priory of Hexham. This will contain an imprint of the 
Black Book of the Monastery, from the original in the pos- 
session of Mr. Beaumont, and all the deeds and grants con- 
nected with the possessions of the house and the local admi- 
nistration of the Regality that it has been possible to recover. 
There will also be in the volume an architectural description 
of the church illustrated with numerous engravings. Tho 
chief renown of Hexham is in its Saxon history, and all the 
remains of that period that have been discovered in tho place 
will be set forth in the volume. 

In addition to these two works, great progress has been 
mado with others that will before long be presented to the 
members of the Society. A second volume of the Memorials 
of Fountains Abbey is now ready for the press; and, through 
the kind munificence of Mr. Akroyd, it will be richly illus- 
trated with engravings. Tho Livos of St. Wilfrid, and 
some other historical pieces, are, we are happy to say, 
being prepared by the Kev. William Stubbs. A third vol- 
ume of Durham and Northumberland Wills (to conclude 
the series) is being collected by the Rev. William Greenwell. 
The Council has also much pleasure in announcing for speedy 
publication the Letters and Household Books of Lord Wil- 
liam Howard of Naworth. Through the great kindness of 
the Earl of Carlisle these memorials of " Belted Will " have 
been placed at tho disposal of the Society. We have been 
accustomed to look upon Lord William merely as a Border 
chieftain, but it is evident that ho was a i>erson of great re- 
finement and taste. In spite of the misfortunes ot himself 
and his family, he found time to gather together a collection 
of old Chronicles and MSS., and ho took care that some of 
them were printed: he made a collection of pictures and 
works of art; ho was an accomplished genealogist; and he 
corresponded with tho famous Camden about Roman altars.

THE SURTEES SOCIETY, 

ESTABLISHED IN THE YEAR 18S4, 

In honour of the late Robert Surtees, of Mainsforth, Esquire, 
the Author of the History of the County Palatine of Durham, 
and in accordance with his pursuits and plans ; having for its 
object the publication of inedited Manuscripts, illustrative of 
the intellectual, the moral, the religious, and the social con- 
dition of those parts of England and Scotland, included on the 
east between the Humber and the Frith of Forth, and on the 
west between the Mersey and the Clyde, a region which con- 
stituted the ancient Kingdom of Northuinbria. 

NEW RULES AGREED UPON IN 1849; REVISED 1863. 

I. The Society shall consist of not more than three hun- 
dred and fifty members. 

II. There shall be a Patron of the Society, who shall be 
President 

III. There shall be twenty-four Vice-Presidents, a Secre- 
tary, and two Treasurers. < 

IV. The Patron, the Vice-Presidents, the Secretary, and 
the Treasurers, shall form the Council, any five of whom, 
including the Secretary and a Treasurer, shall be a quorum 
competent to transact the business of the Society. 

V. The twenty-four Vice-Presidents, the Secretary, and 
the Treasurers, shall be elected at a general meeting, to con- 
tinue in office for three years, and be capable of re-election. 

VI. Any vacancios in the offices of Secretary or Treasurers 
shall be provisionally filled up by the Council, subject to the 
approbation of the next general meeting. 

VIL Three meetings of the Council shall be held in every 
year, on the first Tuesday in the months of March, June, and 
December ; and the place and hour of meeting shall be fixed 
by the Council, and communicated by the Secretary to the 
members of the Council. 

VIII. The meeting in June shall be the anniversary, to 
which all the members of the Society shall be convened by 
the Secrotary. 

IX. The Secretary shall convene extraordinary moetings of 



Digitized by Google 



5 

the Council, on a requisition to that effect, signed by not less 
than tive members of the Council, being presented to him. 

X. Members may be elected by ballot at any one of the 
ordinary meetings, according to priority of application, upon 
being proposed in writing by three existing members. One 
black ball in ten shall exclude. 

XI. Each member shall pay in advance to the Treasurer 
the annual sum of one guinea. If any member's subscription 
shall be in arrear for two years, and he shall neglect to pay 
his subscripton after having been reminded by the Treasurer, 
he shall be regarded as having ceased to be a member of the 
Society. 

XII. The money raised by the Society shall be expended 
in publishing such compositions, in their original language, or 
in a translated form, as come within the scope of this Society, 
without limitation of time with reference to the period of their 
respective authors. All editorial and other expenses to be de- 
frayed by the Society. 

XII L One volume, at least, in a closely printed octavo 
form, shall be supplied to each member of the Society every 
year, free of expense. 

XIV. If the funds of the Society in any year will permit, 
the Council shall be at liberty to print and furnish to the 
members, free of expense, any other volume or volumes of the 
same character, in the same or a different form. 

XV. The number of copies of each publication, and the 
selection of a printer and publisher, shall be left to the Council, 
who shall also fix the price at which the copies not furnished 
to members shall be sold to the public. 

XVI. The armorial bearings of Mr. Surtees and some other 
characteristic decoration connecting the Society with his 
name, shall be used in each publication. 

XVII. A list of the officers and members, together with an 
account of the receipts and expenses of the Society, shall be 
made up even' year to the time of the annual meeting, and 
shall be submitted to the Society to be printed and published 
with the next succeeding volume. 

XVIII. No alteration shall be made in these rides except 
at an annual meeting. Notice of any such alteration shall be 
given, at least as early as the ordinary meeting of the Council 
immediately preceding, to be communicated to each member 
of the Society.
